hero.headline: North Palm Beach celebrates Independence Day with fireworks and America 250 events at country club
hero.teaser: North Palm Beach residents and visitors will celebrate Independence Day with family-friendly activities, live entertainment and fireworks at North Palm Beach Country Club and The Clubhouse on July 4.
hero.body:
The free community event includes a pool party, lawn games, live music, a barbecue buffet and a fireworks finale scheduled for 9 p.m. Organizers say this years event also recognizes Americas 250th anniversary, bringing an added sense of celebration to the annual holiday tradition in Palm Beach County.

The festivities begin with a community pool party from 11 a.m. at the country club pool area. Guests can enjoy a water slide, DJ entertainment, games and activities, food and beverages, and a poolside satellite bar. Beginning at 4:30 p.m., families can take part in activities including cornhole, Connect 4, giant Jenga, face painting and lawn games. Live music from Solstice Reign is expected to begin around 6 p.m.

Ashley Shipman, director of parks and recreation, said the golf course will offer one of the best locations to watch the fireworks display. The Clubhouse will also host a Fourth of July barbecue buffet from 4:30 p.m.

cards.headline: Florida moves to bar undocumented students from state colleges and universities as new restrictions advance
cards.body:
Florida education officials this week moved forward with significant new barriers for undocumented students seeking higher education in the state. The State Board of Education voted to advance rules that would prevent undocumented immigrants from enrolling in any of Florida's 28 state colleges and adult education programs. The restrictions would also apply to GED preparation courses, which many students use as a pathway to college or workforce training opportunities.

This action by the State Board of Education follows a similar decision by the state university system's Board of Governors, which approved a plan to bar undocumented students from Florida's public universities starting in the 2027-28 academic year. Students already enrolled at these universities would not be affected by the new policy. Together, these measures represent an escalating effort by state officials to limit educational access for undocumented immigrants, building on Florida's previous decision to eliminate in-state tuition rates for many undocumented students, including those protected under DACA.

Supporters of the restrictions contend that taxpayer-funded educational institutions should be available only to students who are legally present in the United States. However, immigrant advocates and students have voiced strong opposition to the new rules. Alexander Vallejos, a student Dreamer, challenged the restrictions by saying "We're just asking for an opportunity to earn our future through education. Because when Dreamers succeed, Florida succeeds." Advocates argue that the restrictions would deny opportunities to young people who have grown up in Florida and graduated from Florida high schools.

These education policy moves occurred during a week marked by other significant developments in Florida politics. Governor Ron DeSantis announced that Florida would use a new state law to designate organizations as terrorist groups. DeSantis stated the state would seek to designate the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the Muslim Brotherhood, and Antifa, along with more than 90 federally designated foreign terrorist organizations. The law, which took effect July 1, allows the governor and Florida Cabinet to make these designations based on recommendations from state domestic security officials. If approved by the Cabinet, the designations could block public funding and contracts from listed groups and create penalties for providing material support. CAIR and civil rights organizations quickly sued in federal court, arguing that the process violates free speech and due process rights, and that DeSantis cannot unilaterally brand organizations with such designations without judicial review.

cards.headline: Martin County School Board challenges judge's order to reinstate teacher suspended over Charlie Kirk comments
cards.teaser: The Martin County School Board filed a court challenge Thursday against an administrative law judge's recommendation to reinstate a teacher suspended last year .
cards.body:
The Martin County School Board is pushing back against a judge's recommendation to reinstate a teacher suspended last year following controversial social media comments about Charlie Kirk. Matt Theobald, a social studies teacher at Spectrum Academy since 2009, sparked controversy with his comments, which labeled Kirk as racist, misogynistic and a neo-Nazi. In a Thursday court filing, the school board argued Administrative Law Judge Jodi-Ann Vanessa Livingstone erred in recommending Theobald get his job back, saying "numerous findings ... are not based upon competent substantial evidence." The board's attorney claims Theobald's Facebook post about Kirk was a "serious offense" and removing him was appropriate.

In an order issued last month, Livingstone cited a recent Florida Fifth District Court of Appeal ruling that said disciplining a teacher for personal Facebook posts made off school grounds, on personal equipment, with no student involvement, violated the teacher's First Amendment rights. The judge also recommended Theobald be awarded back pay and benefits. According to an investigation report, Theobald admitted writing the comments about Kirk but said they were posted on his mother's private Facebook page "within a discussion among personal acquaintances" and were not intended for public view. After the judge's recommendation, Theobald told WPTV the case raises a larger question about where the line is drawn for teachers speaking outside of school. The school board still has the final say on whether Theobald gets his job back.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds secures $90 million in fundraising and major endorsements as Florida GOP primary approaches
cards.teaser: The Republican gubernatorial candidate launched a $20 million statewide advertising buy and gained support from two DeSantis-appointed statewide officials as the August primary draws closer.
cards.body:
Byron Donalds entered the week as the front-runner in the GOP race to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis, with strengthening momentum. His campaign and affiliated political committee raised more than $90 million this cycle, including more than $23 million in the second quarter. The campaign recently launched a $20 million statewide advertising buy, putting Donalds on television as Florida's August primary approaches. Donalds picked up endorsements from two statewide officials appointed by DeSantis: Attorney General James Uthmeier and Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia. He also has backing from the two incoming legislative leaders, Senate President Jim Boyd and House Speaker Sam Garrison. The endorsements are notable in a primary where DeSantis himself has not endorsed a successor, though several figures connected to his administration have lined up behind Donalds.

While Donalds builds money and institutional support, Lt. Gov. Jay Collins filed a lawsuit challenging Republican candidate James Fishback's eligibility. Collins argues Fishback does not meet Florida's constitutional requirement that a governor live in the state for at least seven years before being elected. The legal complaint points to Fishback's ties to Washington, D.C., including allegations he claimed a D.C. property as a primary residence and voted there in 2020. Fishback denied he is ineligible and accused Collins of trying to damage his campaign. The court fight adds uncertainty to the GOP primary as mail ballots soon go out and the Aug. 18 primary approaches.

cards.headline: Martin County maritime teams prepare for Fourth of July boating surge
cards.teaser: Martin County Maritime Response Unit is deploying two boats with medics on standby as hundreds of boaters hit the waterways for Independence Day weekend.
cards.body:
Hundreds of boaters are expected on Florida waterways this Fourth of July weekend, prompting local maritime safety officials to increase patrols. Lt. Brett Harry with Martin County Maritime Response Unit said his team will have two boats with medics on standby positioned in both the north and south areas of Martin County to respond to emergencies. Harry said the unit is prepared to handle situations ranging from minor injuries like stubbed toes to more serious medical events including cardiac emergencies and potential spinal injuries.

Boaters launching from Sandsprit Park in Martin County on Friday, including Brendan and Ashley Shannon with their young daughter and puppy, emphasized that safety is their top priority on the water. Harry urged all boaters to keep their eyes on the water, designate a sober driver, and pack life vests, whistles and flotation devices before setting sail. "Just have fun and be safe," Harry said of the holiday weekend ahead.

cards.headline: St. Petersburg selects $8.1 billion proposal to redevelop Tropicana Field site with permanent home for Woodson Museum
cards.teaser: The Burg Bid plan calls for purchasing 58 acres of city-owned land for $275 million and transforming the area into a mixed-use district centered around a 13-acre civic park.
cards.body:
St. Petersburg Mayor Ken Welch selected The Burg Bid as the city's preferred path forward for redeveloping Tropicana Field and the surrounding Historic Gas Plant District. Led by Blake Investment Partners and Related Group, the proposal outlines an $8.1 billion plan to transform acres of stadium parking and public land into a mixed-use district with housing, hotels, offices, retail, cultural institutions, workforce training, public art and entertainment space. The team calls for purchasing 58 acres of city-owned land for $275 million and proposes a $20 million deposit when a purchase and sale agreement is executed.

Unlike the previous redevelopment deal centered on a new stadium, The Burg Bid proposal would be organized around Samuel Davis Park, a 13-acre central park serving as a civic and cultural space. The park would include The Woodson African American Museum of Florida, a planned Museum of Public Art, a Discovery Center, event lawns, a playground, a splash pad, café areas, public art and a concert lawn. The Woodson would serve as an anchor and civic landmark for the Gas Plant District, positioned within Samuel Davis Park along a diagonal pedestrian corridor called the Legacy Link. The plan calls for 3,600 income-restricted housing units over a 15-year buildout, with 1,800 units in the Historic Gas Plant District and 1,800 on complementary sites elsewhere in St. Petersburg. The district would be built in three phases lasting approximately five years each, with early development possible before stadium demolition. The Tampa Bay Rays' lease with the city ends after the 2028 season.

hero.headline: Juno Beach weighs cost of replacing fence at JB-7 beach access after resident complaints
hero.teaser: A missing fence at the JB-7 public beach access point has prompted complaints from Colony Condos residents who say beachgoers are trespassing on private property. The Juno Beach Town Council will take up the fence question during budget discussions July 15.
hero.body:
Residents at the Colony Condos are pushing back against summer beachgoers who they say are trespassing on their private property since the town removed a boundary fence in 2023. The town initially took down the fence for safety reasons, leaving only vegetation to mark where the public walkway ends and private land begins. Colony resident Lori Hill described the recurring problem, explaining that beachgoers park in nearby spots and push back bushes to cut through with coolers, fishing rods, and lawn chairs. Hill said the issue intensifies during summer months when random cars fill the parking areas throughout the day.

Hill recalled that when the fence was in place, property lines were unmistakable and trespassing was less common. She noted that residents initially confronted people crossing onto private property, but those interactions often turned hostile. "We used to confront them and tell them this is private property, and they would get pretty rude," Hill said. "So, now what we've just been doing is just calling the police, and they've been coming up and confronting them." The ongoing tensions prompted the condo residents to bring their concerns before the Juno Beach Town Council.

Not all beachgoers acknowledge a significant problem. Michael House, a regular visitor to JB-7, said he accesses the beach from a public parking lot blocks away and has not observed the trespassing issues residents describe. "There's plenty of free parking. If they're damaging property and you know littering and stuff like that might be a different issue," House said. "I have never noticed anyone hopping the fence or the shrubs or anything like that."

During a recent town council meeting, officials clarified that the town has no legal obligation to install a fence. However, Vice Mayor Pro Tem DD Halpern suggested exploring more affordable alternatives to a full replacement. "I understand fencing is expensive, but I'd like to see maybe we can help them with a lower-cost fence or some combination of split rail and shrubs," Halpern said. Hill expressed hope that the town would reinstall some form of boundary to restore clear property lines and protect resident parking areas. The council decided to address the fence replacement question during budget discussions scheduled for July 15, leaving open the possibility that a solution could involve shared costs or hybrid approaches combining different barrier materials.

cards.headline: Riviera Beach named only Florida city to receive 2026 All-America City Award
cards.teaser: Riviera Beach was named one of just 10 communities in the U.S. to receive the 2026 All-America City Award from the National Civic League. The city highlighted programs including the Riviera Beach Youth Council and the Neighborhood Reclaim Home Rehabilitation Program.
cards.body:
Riviera Beach was named one of just 10 U.S. communities to receive the 2026 All-America City Award from the National Civic League, making it the only Florida city selected for the honor this year. The prestigious award recognizes communities that bring residents, local government, businesses and organizations together to solve local challenges and create lasting change. The award was announced during the National Civic League conference in Denver, where Riviera Beach leaders presented the city's efforts to strengthen community engagement. Mayor Douglas Lawson called the recognition a proud moment for the city. "Little old Riviera Beach is one of the biggest, brightest, shining stars," Lawson said. He noted the city earned the award through a long-term effort to revitalize Riviera Beach and improve quality of life for residents.

Riviera Beach's application highlighted several programs designed to increase civic participation and neighborhood investment, including the Riviera Beach Youth Council, which helps high school students become involved in civic leadership and advocacy, the Citizens Leadership Academy with a 98% completion rate, and the Neighborhood Reclaim Home Rehabilitation Program, which provides mini-grants to help longtime homeowners make critical repairs. Councilwoman KaShamba Miller-Anderson credited residents for the honor, saying the award reinforces the city's positive momentum and brings back community pride. The All-America City Award has been presented annually since 1949 and is considered one of the nation's most respected civic honors.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County schools earn third consecutive 'A' rating with record 93.5% graduation rate
cards.teaser: The School District of Palm Beach County received an 'A' rating from the state for the third consecutive year. The district achieved a record-setting 93.5% graduation rate, with 143 schools rated A or B.
cards.body:
For the third year in a row, the School District of Palm Beach County earned an "A" rating from the Florida Department of Education. This year, 143 district-operated schools, or 84%, received either an "A" or "B" rating, up from 120 schools the previous year. School districts and schools receive letter grades based on student performance on state tests, graduation rates and student performance on advanced coursework. The district also achieved a record-setting 93.5% graduation rate. District leaders noted that 86% of seniors participated in college-level coursework, including Advanced Placement, International Baccalaureate, Cambridge Advanced International Certificate of Education, or Dual Enrollment courses. Additionally, 144 recent graduates earned an associate degree alongside their high school diploma.

One of the district's notable successes came from S.D. Spady Elementary School in Delray Beach, which jumped from a "C" rating to an "A" rating this year. Principal Rona Tata has led the school for 15 years, following five years as assistant principal. Three years ago, the school began modifying its early childhood curriculum program, which serves students starting at age 3 and combines with kindergarten. Spady Elementary was one of four district schools to improve from a "C" to an "A" rating this year, along with Dwight D. Eisenhower K-8, Glade View Elementary and West Gate Elementary.

cards.headline: Boca Raton Community High School band to represent Florida at National Independence Day Parade
cards.teaser: The Boca Raton Community High School band will march in Washington, D.C.'s National Independence Day Parade on July 4. The students will march a full mile along the National Mall, representing the entire state of Florida.
cards.body:
The Boca Raton Community High School band earned a coveted spot in Washington, D.C.'s National Independence Day Parade, representing the entire state of Florida. On July 4 at 10:30 a.m., the students will march a full mile along the National Mall, from Constitution Avenue to Independence Avenue. Only bands nominated by state officials receive invitations to this prestigious event. Junior Lola Cabezas acknowledged the pressure of performing for millions of viewers. "There are millions, if not billions, of people watching," Cabezas said. "It's a lot of pressure, but I think we'll be able to rise to the occasion." She also highlighted the physical demands of marching band, explaining that students must simultaneously play instruments, breathe properly, and maintain consistent sound while walking.

Senior Stephin Restivo said the team is focused on executing every detail. "Just focusing on the marching, the timing of everything. Everybody is going to be able to see it," Restivo said. "Everyone will be able to see what the Boca High band is capable of." Band Director Jenn Girdlestone expressed confidence in her students heading into the national spotlight. For senior Lily Schaffer, the opportunity demonstrates the program's growth. "Getting to do this is an amazing opportunity," Schaffer said. "It shows how much we've grown and showcases what we do here, because this program is so amazing." The parade will be streamed live on YouTube.

cards.headline: Breast cancer patient and surgeon speak out after insurance denies reconstruction surgery hours before procedure
cards.teaser: Beth Clark, 48, and her plastic surgeon are speaking out after Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield denied coverage for a reconstruction procedure less than 24 hours before it was scheduled. The denial involved surgical mesh called GalaFlex, which the insurer considers investigational.
cards.body:
Beth Clark, 48, was diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma three months ago and underwent a full double bilateral mastectomy. Less than 24 hours before her scheduled reconstruction surgery, her insurance company, Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield, denied coverage for the procedure. According to her denial letter, the surgery involved a surgical mesh called GalaFlex, which the insurer classified as "investigational" with "no or not enough proof it improves health." While GalaFlex is FDA-approved for some uses in the body, it is not approved for breast reconstruction and remains considered off-label and experimental. In a 2023 letter to health care providers, the FDA stated that the treatment's "efficacy and safety for breast cancer patients have not been determined."

Despite the denial, Clark received her reconstruction surgery with GalaFlex mesh a little more than a week later, thanks to her plastic surgeon, Dr. Alicia Billington. Billington uses GalaFlex on most of her breast reconstruction patients and believes it is less risky than other options with proven success. Last year, after investigative reporting by Katie LaGrone and Matthew Apthorp, Cigna became the first and only major insurer to start approving GalaFlex for breast reconstruction. Clark and Billington continue fighting Anthem's denial, and a new bill has been introduced to modernize the Women's Health and Cancer Rights Act.

cards.headline: Fourth of July cookout costs rise 4% this year, summer meal for 10 now costs $73.82
cards.teaser: A holiday meal for 10 now costs $73.82, up 4% from a year ago, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation's Summer Cookout Cost Survey. Ground beef is up 5.5%, buns are up 7.7%, and strawberries are up 12.4%.
cards.body:
According to the American Farm Bureau Federation's Summer Cookout Cost Survey, a holiday meal for 10 now costs $73.82, up 4% from a year ago. The survey attributes the increase to inflation, with ground beef prices up 5.5% and buns up 7.7%. Strawberries have seen the steepest jump at 12.4%, hit hard by a Florida frost, while ice cream prices are up 5.3%.

However, not all items have increased in cost. Potato prices are down this year, benefiting those planning to serve potato chips and salads. Corn prices have fluctuated, though locally grown corn from the Glades can offer the best value. Budgeting expert Andrea Woroch recommends shopping strategically by comparing prices across stores to find the best deals for groceries on your list. She also emphasized that families should focus on cutting down food waste by starting with a meal plan.

hero.headline: Hobe Sound woman killed in house fire had birthday on Fourth of July
hero.teaser: Misty Dawn White died Monday in a house fire that investigators believe was caused by an electrical issue. Friends are now raising funds for her fiance, who lost his only child in an earlier tragedy.
hero.body:
Misty Dawn White, 46, died in a house fire at her Hobe Sound home on Monday. Investigators from the sheriff's office are examining the blaze, with preliminary findings suggesting an electrical issue may have caused it. The investigation is still ongoing as authorities work to determine the exact cause of the fire.

White's fiancé, Mark, received support from friends and family following the tragedy. Nina Fenn, who had been friends with White for eight years, learned of the death through a phone call from Mark. "We received a call from Mark stating that Misty had passed away in a fire," Fenn said. Since the fire destroyed many of their belongings, friends launched a fundraiser to help Mark rebuild. Fenn described the situation as "completely a state of devastation."

Fenn spoke about White's character and how she wants her to be remembered. "Misty was a Christian woman. She loved gardening and plants. She plays the piano," Fenn said. "She was always the first to lend a hand. She loves kids; she loves her kids. She loves people." According to Fenn, White was known for her generosity and willingness to help others. The loss has been particularly difficult for those close to her, especially considering Mark's previous tragedy. "Mark lost his one and only child, Jacob, and lost him tragically. So, I just am trying whatever I can to support him," Fenn said.

The timing of White's death adds another layer of sadness for those who knew her. White's birthday fell on the Fourth of July, meaning she passed away just days before turning another year older. "Misty's birthday is the Fourth of July. So, she passed just a few days before her birthday," Fenn said. Despite the heartbreak of losing White so close to her birthday, those who knew her are holding onto her memory. "She's always been a good soul to me. She'll always be in our hearts," Fenn said.

cards.headline: Stuart downtown dock closes Sunday for $3 million renovation
cards.teaser: The public dock will close July 6 for a year-long renovation that will nearly double its capacity from 18 to 44 boat slips.
cards.body:
Stuart's downtown public dock will close July 6 for renovations projected to be complete by next Fourth of July. The $3 million project will nearly double the dock's capacity, expanding from 18 to 44 slips for both motorized and non-motorized vessels. The renovation will include a 7,500 square foot fixed dock, a 1,400 square foot floating dock and a smaller floating platform. The project is funded by a state grant and transportation impact fees.

Stuart Mayor Sean Reed said the upgrades are designed to prevent storm damage during hurricanes and major storms. More than 1,400 boaters use the dock annually. During the closure, the city is working to accommodate businesses relying on the dock. Tiki Taxi & Cruises, which operates off the dock, will be allowed to build a gate at the non-floating section of the dock to continue operations. Austin Kuyrkendall, director of operations for Tiki Taxi & Cruises, said modernizing and expanding the dock will be great for the city and for his business.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie moves forward with Florida Turnpike interchange at Midway Road
cards.teaser: The Port St. Lucie City Council approved giving 7 acres of land to the Florida Department of Transportation to build a partial interchange on the Turnpike as part of the Midway Road Widening Project.
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of an ordinance last month to give 7 acres of land to the Florida Department of Transportation for a partial interchange at the Florida Turnpike. Scott Samples, strategic communications manager for Port St. Lucie, said the city has a significant gap between the entrances and exits to the Turnpike currently in Port St. Lucie. Samples explained the interchange addresses accessibility and growth in the city, stating it will help accommodate growth already occurring and growth expected over the next 20 to 50 years.

FDOT has been constructing the $95 million Midway Road Widening Project to address congestion and safety concerns. Crews are currently working on the first phase, widening the road from two lanes to four lanes from Selvitz Road to Jenkins Road. The second widening phase, from Jenkins Road to Glades Cut Off Road, remains in the design phase with construction anticipated to begin in Summer 2027. The partial interchange is also still in the design phase. The project will include bike and pedestrian paths along with sidewalks. The city council will vote on final approval to give the land at an upcoming meeting.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach considers elevated self-driving transit system connecting airport to downtown
cards.teaser: California-based Glydways will present a proposal to Palm Beach County commissioners Tuesday for an elevated network of autonomous vehicles that could cut the trip between downtown and the airport to less than 10 minutes.
cards.body:
Glydways, a California-based autonomous transit company, is proposing an elevated network of self-driving vehicles to connect downtown West Palm Beach to President Donald J. Trump International Airport. The company will present the proposal to Palm Beach County commissioners Tuesday for initial consideration. Supporters said the system could dramatically improve mobility by connecting the airport to the convention center, nearby Brightline and Tri-Rail stations.

Small autonomous electric vehicles carrying four to six passengers would travel along a dedicated elevated guideway built above existing roads. The system would bypass traffic congestion entirely, potentially cutting the trip between downtown and the airport to less than 10 minutes. Glydways estimates travel times of seven minutes or less between the convention center and airport and roughly one to two minutes between Tri-Rail and the convention center. Senior Vice President Brian Gettinger said the system would cost a small fraction of a traditional light rail system, which has previously carried estimates of $400 million to $500 million per mile in South Florida. Funding could potentially come from Palm Beach County, the City of West Palm Beach, the Florida Department of Transportation, federal transit grants and public-private partnerships. Tuesday's County Commission meeting is expected to determine whether the county should formally evaluate the proposal.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County deputies make 15 DUI arrests in holiday enforcement
cards.teaser: Deputies targeted impaired driving in St. Lucie County ahead of the Fourth of July weekend.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County deputies made 15 DUI arrests as part of a targeted enforcement effort to reduce impaired driving ahead of the Fourth of July holiday weekend. The arrests were part of an operation to keep roads safe during the holiday period when traffic and alcohol consumption typically increase.

The enforcement effort comes as hundreds of residents and visitors are expected to travel throughout St. Lucie County for Independence Day celebrations. Law enforcement agencies across the Treasure Coast have increased patrols and checkpoints during major holiday weekends to address impaired driving.

hero.headline: Riviera Beach named only Florida city to win 2026 All-America City Award
hero.teaser: Riviera Beach was selected as one of just 10 communities in the U.S. to receive the 2026 All-America City Award from the National Civic League, making it the only Florida city to earn the honor this year.
hero.body:
Riviera Beach has earned national recognition as one of only 10 U.S. communities selected for the 2026 All-America City Award from the National Civic League. The announcement was made during the National Civic League conference in Denver, where Riviera Beach leaders presented the city's community engagement efforts to judges. As the sole Florida city receiving the award this year, Riviera Beach joins Chelsea, Massachusetts; Franklin, Tennessee; Harlingen, Texas; Montgomery, Alabama; Morrisville, North Carolina; Norfolk, Virginia; North Charleston, South Carolina; Roanoke, Virginia; and Woodburn, Oregon as this year's honorees. The award recognizes communities that unite residents, local government, businesses and organizations to address local challenges and create meaningful change.

Mayor Douglas Lawson expressed pride in the achievement, describing Riviera Beach as "one of the biggest, brightest, shining stars." He credited the city's success to years of deliberate effort aimed at revitalizing the community and enhancing quality of life for residents. Lawson noted that residents are witnessing the transformation that city leaders envisioned. The recognition reflects an extended commitment to strengthening civic health, building trust between residents and government, and ensuring residents actively shape the city's direction. Councilwoman KaShamba Miller-Anderson emphasized that the award belongs to the entire community, stating "This award is a tribute to the heart and determination of our residents. Every event we host, every project we complete, and every challenge we overcome happens because our community shows up for one another."

The city's application showcased three signature programs demonstrating civic participation and community investment. The Riviera Beach Youth Council engages high school students in civic leadership and advocacy. The Citizens Leadership Academy, a civic education program, boasts a 98 percent completion rate. The Neighborhood Reclaim Home Rehabilitation Program provides mini-grants to longtime homeowners for necessary repairs. Miller-Anderson stated that these initiatives reflect the city's commitment to treating civic engagement as an ongoing partnership involving government, residents, faith groups, schools and community organizations. She noted that the city continues developing innovative approaches to ensure residents feel invested in the city's progress.

The All-America City Award, presented annually since 1949, ranks among the nation's most respected civic honors. City leaders view the designation as validation of Riviera Beach's progress and momentum. The award positions the community for future growth and opportunities while signaling to the nation that collaboration and resident involvement drive results in Riviera Beach. Officials emphasized that the recognition reinforces community pride and demonstrates the city's commitment to shaping a stronger future through collective effort.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie approves land transfer for new Florida Turnpike interchange on Midway Road
cards.teaser: The Port St.
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of an ordinance last month to transfer 7 acres of land to the Florida Department of Transportation for a partial interchange on Florida's Turnpike in St. Lucie County. Scott Samples, strategic communications manager for Port St. Lucie, said the interchange addresses a significant gap between the current Turnpike entrances and exits in the city. According to Samples, the project aims to accommodate growth projected over the next 20 to 50 years. The $95 million Midway Road Widening Project includes this interchange along with road improvements to address congestion and safety.

Crews are currently working on the first phase of the project, widening Midway Road from two lanes to four lanes between Selvitz Road and Jenkins Road. The second widening phase from Jenkins Road to Glades Cut Off Road remains in the design phase with construction anticipated to begin in Summer 2027. FDOT is also improving the Turnpike bridge and designing the partial interchange, which is still in the design phase. The project will add bike and pedestrian paths along with sidewalks. The city council will vote on final approval of the land transfer at an upcoming meeting.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound woman dies in home fire, community raises funds for fiance
cards.teaser: Misty Dawn White, 46, was found dead Monday after a fire broke out inside her Hobe Sound home. Preliminary findings from the sheriff's office point to an electrical issue as a possible cause.
cards.body:
Misty Dawn White, 46, was found dead Monday after a fire broke out inside her home in Hobe Sound. Preliminary findings from the sheriff's office point to an electrical issue as a possible cause. The fire remains under investigation. Nina Fenn, a friend of White's for eight years, learned of the death through a phone call from White's fiancé Mark, who told her that Misty had passed away in a fire.

Friends have launched a fundraiser to help Mark rebuild after the flames destroyed many of his and White's belongings. Fenn described the scene as completely a state of devastation. She remembered White as a Christian woman who loved gardening, plants, and playing the piano, and was always the first to lend a hand. Fenn said the loss is compounded by grief Mark has already endured, noting that he previously lost his one and only child, Jacob, tragically. White's birthday is July 4, meaning she passed just a few days before her birthday. Fenn said White's memory will live on in the hearts of those who loved her.

cards.headline: Martin County School Board fights judge's order to reinstate teacher suspended over Charlie Kirk comments
cards.teaser: The Martin County School Board is pushing back against an administrative law judge's recommendation to reinstate Matt Theobald, a Spectrum Academy teacher suspended last year over Facebook comments about Charlie Kirk.
cards.body:
The Martin County School Board is pushing back against a judge's recommendation to reinstate Matt Theobald, a social studies teacher at Spectrum Academy since 2009, who was suspended last year following controversial social media comments about Charlie Kirk. In a Thursday court filing, the school board argued Administrative Law Judge Jodi-Ann Vanessa Livingstone erred in recommending Theobald get his job back, saying "numerous findings ... are not based upon competent substantial evidence." The board's attorney claims Theobald's Facebook post about Kirk, which labeled Kirk as racist, misogynistic and a neo-Nazi, was a "serious offense" and removing him was appropriate.

In an order issued last month, Livingstone cited a recent Florida Fifth District Court of Appeal ruling that said disciplining a teacher for personal Facebook posts made off school grounds, on personal equipment, with no student involvement, violated the teacher's First Amendment rights. The judge also recommended Theobald be awarded back pay and benefits. According to an investigation report obtained by WPTV, Theobald admitted writing the comments about Kirk but said they were posted on his mother's private Facebook page "within a discussion among personal acquaintances" and were not intended for public view. The school board still has the final say on whether Theobald gets his job back.

cards.headline: Fourth of July cookout costs rise 4% this year across Treasure Coast
cards.teaser: A holiday meal for 10 now costs $73.82, up 4% from a year ago, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation's Summer Cookout Cost Survey.
cards.body:
The Fourth of July tradition of cookouts, grilling and picnics comes with a higher price tag this year. According to the American Farm Bureau Federation's Summer Cookout Cost Survey, a holiday meal for 10 now costs $73.82, up 4% from a year ago. Inflation is driving the increases across multiple items. Ground beef prices are up 5.5%, buns are up 7.7%, strawberries hit hard by a Florida frost are up 12.4%, and ice cream is up 5.3%.

Not all cookout staples have increased in cost. Potato prices are down this year, benefiting those planning potato chips and salads. Corn prices have fluctuated, though locally grown corn from the Glades can offer the best deals. Budgeting expert Andrea Woroch recommends comparing stores to find the best deals for groceries on your list, cutting down food waste, and starting with a meal plan.

cards.headline: Breast cancer patient speaks out after Anthem Blue Cross denies reconstruction surgery hours before procedure
cards.teaser: Beth Clark, 48, was denied coverage for a reconstruction procedure less than 24 hours before it was scheduled. Her insurance company, Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield, said the surgical mesh involved is still considered investigational.
cards.body:
Beth Clark, 48, was diagnosed three months ago with invasive ductal carcinoma, the most common type of breast cancer. She underwent a full double bilateral mastectomy with reconstruction, but less than 24 hours before her reconstruction surgery, her insurance company, Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield, denied coverage for the procedure. According to her denial letter, the surgery involved a surgical mesh called GalaFlex, which the insurer considers investigational with insufficient proof that it improves health. GalaFlex is a synthetic surgical mesh that is popular among plastic surgeons and FDA-approved for some uses in the body, but it is not approved for breast reconstruction and remains an off-label, investigational treatment. In a 2023 letter to health care providers, the FDA stated that the efficacy and safety of GalaFlex for breast cancer patients have not been determined.

Despite the denial, Clark received her reconstruction surgery with GalaFlex mesh a little more than a week ago, thanks to her plastic surgeon, Dr. Alicia Billington. Billington believes insurance companies should reconsider their stance, stating the product gives her patients the least amount of complications. Anthem responded that it regularly reviews coverage policies to ensure they are based on medical evidence and aligned with treatment standards, but without FDA approval, the mesh does not meet their coverage requirements. Clark and Billington are still fighting the denial as a new bill has been introduced to modernize the Women's Health and Cancer Rights Act, a federal law designed to protect breast cancer patients from being denied treatments.

cards.headline: Boca Raton Community High School band selected to represent Florida at National Independence Day Parade
cards.teaser: The Boca Raton Community High School band has earned a coveted spot in Washington, D.C.'s National Independence Day Parade and will represent the entire state of Florida on July 4.
cards.body:
The Boca Raton Community High School band has earned a coveted spot in Washington, D.C.'s National Independence Day Parade and will represent the entire state of Florida. On July 4 at 10:30 a.m., the students will march a full mile along the National Mall, from Constitution Avenue to Independence Avenue. Only bands nominated by state officials get invited to this prestigious event. The parade will be streamed live on YouTube.

Junior Lola Cabezas said there are millions, if not billions, of people watching and acknowledged it's a lot of pressure, but believes the band will rise to the occasion. She explained the physical demands of marching band, noting students must play, breathe, and walk while maintaining consistent sound without hearing their steps in the music. Senior Stephin Restivo said the team is laser-focused on the marching and timing of everything, knowing everyone will be able to see what the Boca High band is capable of. Band Director Jenn Girdlestone said she has full confidence in her students that they'll put their best foot forward and represent the country well. Senior Lily Schaffer said making it to D.C. shows how much the program has grown and showcases what they do at Boca Raton.

hero.headline: Saint Andrew's Scots football targets state title after 10-2 season and district championship
hero.body:
The Saint Andrew's Scots football team is focused on achieving a state championship during the 2026 fall season following a successful 10-2 campaign last year that included a district title. Despite finishing with an impressive regular season record, the team's exit in the second round of the playoffs motivated players and coaches to aim higher this year.

Head coach Jimmy Robertson emphasized the program's advantages heading into the season. "Most of these seniors are four-year seniors. I mean, if not the majority of them came from the middle school as well. So they know how things are run. They had a lot of success in their career, and hopefully their senior year is the best season that we've had," Robertson said. The coaching staff believes this experienced senior class, combined with their familiarity with the program's system, positions the team well for a breakthrough season.

To prepare for their elevated ambitions, the Scots have intentionally scheduled stronger opponents for the upcoming fall. Senior Jack Williams explained the reasoning behind this approach. "We knew that we wanted to take our program to the next level. So we really have a challenging schedule for this year because we wanna compete. That's what we wanna do and we wanna take that next level, and it's by playing against really good teams that we do that and attract new people," Williams said. This strategy reflects the team's desire to compete against top-level competition and build momentum heading into postseason play.

The team's definition of success this season goes beyond regular season performance. Senior Jack Whelche stressed the importance of advancing deeper into the playoffs. "A better year is just gonna be going farther in the playoffs. Obviously we wanna go undefeated in the season, but that doesn't matter if we keep losing in the second round of the playoffs. We just gotta go farther than that, that's all that matters," Whelche said. As the team prepares during summer workouts, players like senior Edmyer St. Jean view the training sessions as motivation for the season ahead. "It just adds up every day as something like to look forward to. Work harder so we can see the results when we come off the season positive and break our record," St. Jean said. The Scots are using their offseason training to build the momentum they believe will carry them toward their state title goal.

cards.headline: Martin County maritime teams prepare for Fourth of July boating surge
cards.teaser: Martin County Maritime Response Unit is deploying two boats with medics on standby as hundreds of boaters hit the waterways for Independence Day weekend.
cards.body:
Hundreds of boaters are expected on Florida waterways this Fourth of July weekend, prompting local maritime safety officials to increase patrols. Lt. Brett Harry with Martin County Maritime Response Unit said his team will have two boats with medics on standby positioned in both the north and south areas of Martin County to respond to emergencies. Harry said the unit is prepared to handle situations ranging from minor injuries like stubbed toes to more serious medical events including cardiac emergencies and potential spinal injuries.

Boaters launching from Sandsprit Park in Martin County on Friday, including Brendan and Ashley Shannon with their young daughter and puppy, emphasized that safety is their top priority on the water. Harry urged all boaters to keep their eyes on the water, designate a sober driver, and pack life vests, whistles and flotation devices before setting sail. "Just have fun and be safe," Harry said of the holiday weekend ahead.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound community supports man after fiancée dies in Monday home fire
cards.teaser: Friends launched a fundraiser to help Mark rebuild after a fire killed his fiancée Misty Dawn White and destroyed their belongings in Hobe Sound.
cards.body:
Misty Dawn White, 46, was found dead Monday after a fire broke out inside the Hobe Sound home she shared with her fiancé Mark. White's birthday was July 4, just days after her death. Fenn said White's memory will endure among those who knew her. "She's always been a good soul to me. She'll always be in our hearts," Fenn said.

cards.headline: Riviera Beach named only Florida city to win 2026 All-America City Award

Riviera Beach was named one of just 10 communities in the U.S. to receive the 2026 All-America City Award from the National Civic League, making it the only Florida city selected for the honor this year. The award was announced during the National Civic League conference in Denver, where Riviera Beach leaders presented the city's efforts to strengthen community engagement. Mayor Douglas Lawson said the city earned the award through a long-term effort to revitalize Riviera Beach and improve quality of life for residents. Lawson stated that residents are seeing the changes and the revitalization that the city set out to accomplish years ago.

The city's application highlighted several civic engagement programs, including the Riviera Beach Youth Council, which helps high school students become involved in civic leadership, the Citizens Leadership Academy with a 98% completion rate, and the Neighborhood Reclaim Home Rehabilitation Program that provides mini-grants to longtime homeowners for critical repairs. hero.headline: North Palm Beach celebrates Independence Day with fireworks and America 250 events at country club
hero.teaser: North Palm Beach residents and visitors will celebrate Independence Day with family-friendly activities, live entertainment and fireworks at North Palm Beach Country Club and The Clubhouse on July 4.
hero.body:
The free community event includes a pool party, lawn games, live music, a barbecue buffet and a fireworks finale scheduled for 9 p.m. Organizers say this years event also recognizes Americas 250th anniversary, bringing an added sense of celebration to the annual holiday tradition in Palm Beach County.

The festivities begin with a community pool party from 11 a.m. at the country club pool area. Guests can enjoy a water slide, DJ entertainment, games and activities, food and beverages, and a poolside satellite bar. Beginning at 4:30 p.m., families can take part in activities including cornhole, Connect 4, giant Jenga, face painting and lawn games. Live music from Solstice Reign is expected to begin around 6 p.m.

Ashley Shipman, director of parks and recreation, said the golf course will offer one of the best locations to watch the fireworks display. The Clubhouse will also host a Fourth of July barbecue buffet from 4:30 p.m.

cards.headline: Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach offers sea turtle nesting season programs through September
cards.body:
Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach is offering educational and interactive programs during peak sea turtle nesting season through September. The center invites guests to participate in guided Turtle Walks, the Hatchling Discovery Program, Hatchling Releases, Tidal Tots and Plastic Free July Community Action Day. These seasonal experiences are designed to give visitors an opportunity to learn about sea turtle conservation along one of the world's busiest sea turtle nesting beaches.

The Turtle Walk program allows participants to observe the nesting process while learning about sea turtle biology, conservation and ongoing research efforts. Educational demonstrations during the programs may include the use of red-light headlamps, amber lighting, night scopes and research tag scanning equipment. The center's education and research departments work together during nesting season to collect and analyze data related to nesting activity and hatchling success. Sea turtle nesting season in Florida typically runs from March through October. Conservation groups encourage beachgoers to turn off beachfront lighting at night, properly dispose of trash and avoid disturbing nesting turtles or hatchlings. Registration information and program details are available through Loggerhead Marinelife Center.

hero.headline: Florida moves to bar undocumented students from state colleges and universities as new restrictions advance
hero.body:
Florida education officials this week moved forward with significant new barriers for undocumented students seeking higher education in the state. The State Board of Education voted to advance rules that would prevent undocumented immigrants from enrolling in any of Florida's 28 state colleges and adult education programs. The restrictions would also apply to GED preparation courses, which many students use as a pathway to college or workforce training opportunities.

This action by the State Board of Education follows a similar decision by the state university system's Board of Governors, which approved a plan to bar undocumented students from Florida's public universities starting in the 2027-28 academic year. Students already enrolled at these universities would not be affected by the new policy. Together, these measures represent an escalating effort by state officials to limit educational access for undocumented immigrants, building on Florida's previous decision to eliminate in-state tuition rates for many undocumented students, including those protected under DACA.

Supporters of the restrictions contend that taxpayer-funded educational institutions should be available only to students who are legally present in the United States. However, immigrant advocates and students have voiced strong opposition to the new rules. Alexander Vallejos, a student Dreamer, challenged the restrictions by saying "We're just asking for an opportunity to earn our future through education. Because when Dreamers succeed, Florida succeeds." Advocates argue that the restrictions would deny opportunities to young people who have grown up in Florida and graduated from Florida high schools.

These education policy moves occurred during a week marked by other significant developments in Florida politics. Governor Ron DeSantis announced that Florida would use a new state law to designate organizations as terrorist groups. DeSantis stated the state would seek to designate the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the Muslim Brotherhood, and Antifa, along with more than 90 federally designated foreign terrorist organizations. The law, which took effect July 1, allows the governor and Florida Cabinet to make these designations based on recommendations from state domestic security officials. If approved by the Cabinet, the designations could block public funding and contracts from listed groups and create penalties for providing material support. CAIR and civil rights organizations quickly sued in federal court, arguing that the process violates free speech and due process rights, and that DeSantis cannot unilaterally brand organizations with such designations without judicial review.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds secures $90 million in fundraising and major endorsements as Florida GOP primary approaches
cards.teaser: The Republican gubernatorial candidate launched a $20 million statewide advertising buy and gained support from two DeSantis-appointed statewide officials as the August primary draws closer.
cards.body:
Byron Donalds entered the week as the front-runner in the GOP race to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis, with strengthening momentum. His campaign and affiliated political committee raised more than $90 million this cycle, including more than $23 million in the second quarter. The campaign recently launched a $20 million statewide advertising buy, putting Donalds on television as Florida's August primary approaches. Donalds picked up endorsements from two statewide officials appointed by DeSantis: Attorney General James Uthmeier and Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia. He also has backing from the two incoming legislative leaders, Senate President Jim Boyd and House Speaker Sam Garrison. The endorsements are notable in a primary where DeSantis himself has not endorsed a successor, though several figures connected to his administration have lined up behind Donalds.

While Donalds builds money and institutional support, Lt. Gov. Jay Collins filed a lawsuit challenging Republican candidate James Fishback's eligibility. Collins argues Fishback does not meet Florida's constitutional requirement that a governor live in the state for at least seven years before being elected. The legal complaint points to Fishback's ties to Washington, D.C., including allegations he claimed a D.C. property as a primary residence and voted there in 2020. Fishback denied he is ineligible and accused Collins of trying to damage his campaign. The court fight adds uncertainty to the GOP primary as mail ballots soon go out and the Aug. 18 primary approaches.

cards.headline: DeSantis allies accuse Jay Collins' wife of running anonymous social media accounts critical of governor
cards.teaser: Multiple social media accounts were deactivated after prominent DeSantis communications veterans presented evidence tying them to Lt. Gov. Jay Collins' wife Layla Collins.
cards.body:
Multiple X accounts were suddenly deactivated after allegations they were tied to Layla Collins, wife of Lt. Gov. Jay Collins. The accusations came from prominent veterans of Gov. Ron DeSantis' communications team, including Christina Pushaw, a communications specialist in the Governor's Office, and Jeremy Redfern, Deputy Chief of Staff to Attorney General James Uthmeier. Pushaw shared information posted by Promota CEO Robert Salvador showing that the account @FSUdude01670 appeared connected to a phone number similar to a known number and email used by Layla Collins. Screenshots verified through two-factor authentication showed an attempt to gain access triggered a message to an email address with letters starred out and to a phone number with only the last digits showing.

Pushaw identified a second account, @bobnamy1, that she said also appeared tied to Layla Collins. She noted the content suggested the account existed entirely to advance Jay Collins' political ambitions as he runs for Governor. "Account content is entirely comprised of two types of posts: Promoting Jay Collins, and attacking people who didn't endorse Jay, including the governor," Pushaw posted. Redfern also criticized the accounts publicly, stating "The FSUDude account was tied directly to her personal cell phone number." After both officials leveled their criticisms publicly, both accounts were deactivated. DeSantis appointed Jay Collins as Lieutenant Governor last year, but has declined to endorse a preferred successor in the Governor's race.

cards.headline: St. Petersburg selects $8.1 billion proposal to redevelop Tropicana Field site with permanent home for Woodson Museum
cards.teaser: The Burg Bid plan calls for purchasing 58 acres of city-owned land for $275 million and transforming the area into a mixed-use district centered around a 13-acre civic park.
cards.body:
St. Petersburg Mayor Ken Welch selected The Burg Bid as the city's preferred path forward for redeveloping Tropicana Field and the surrounding Historic Gas Plant District. Led by Blake Investment Partners and Related Group, the proposal outlines an $8.1 billion plan to transform acres of stadium parking and public land into a mixed-use district with housing, hotels, offices, retail, cultural institutions, workforce training, public art and entertainment space. The team calls for purchasing 58 acres of city-owned land for $275 million and proposes a $20 million deposit when a purchase and sale agreement is executed.

Unlike the previous redevelopment deal centered on a new stadium, The Burg Bid proposal would be organized around Samuel Davis Park, a 13-acre central park serving as a civic and cultural space. The park would include The Woodson African American Museum of Florida, a planned Museum of Public Art, a Discovery Center, event lawns, a playground, a splash pad, café areas, public art and a concert lawn. The Woodson would serve as an anchor and civic landmark for the Gas Plant District, positioned within Samuel Davis Park along a diagonal pedestrian corridor called the Legacy Link. The plan calls for 3,600 income-restricted housing units over a 15-year buildout, with 1,800 units in the Historic Gas Plant District and 1,800 on complementary sites elsewhere in St. Petersburg. The district would be built in three phases lasting approximately five years each, with early development possible before stadium demolition. The Tampa Bay Rays' lease with the city ends after the 2028 season.

cards.headline: Secretary of State Cord Byrd asks court to keep Paula Stark off ballot after incomplete qualifying paperwork
cards.teaser: Five state employees submitted sworn declarations saying Stark's treasurer never submitted the required Form 6 disclosure and was not accidentally handed it back during last-minute filing.
cards.body:
Secretary of State Cord Byrd is asking Leon Circuit Court to keep Paula Stark off the ballot after she submitted incomplete qualifying materials less than 30 minutes before the noon deadline on June 12. In his response to her lawsuit, Byrd challenged Stark's claims about a paperwork mix-up, noting that she and her treasurer, Joel Davis, could have exercised greater care. Five state employees gave sworn written court declarations stating that Davis never submitted the crucial Form 6 nor was he accidentally handed it back when he submitted the rest of the paperwork in the final hour of the qualifying window. Form 6 is a public disclosure of financial interests.

Three weeks after the qualifying deadline passed, Stark still has not submitted Form 6, according to Election Records Division Bureau Chief Erica Ikay Reeve. Reeve said Stark was one of 12 candidates who did not properly turn in Form 6, though half of them corrected the problems and still qualified. Reeve also cited Stark's pattern of paperwork issues, including campaign finance reports filed over one month late, excessive contributions, an incorrect address on file, and unpaid fines. The state revoked Stark's Friends of Paula political committee in November over $16,000 in unpaid fines from missed campaign finance deadlines. If Stark is removed from the ballot, the August Primary for House District 47 would be open to all voters choosing between Democrats Jorge Figueroa and Anthony Nieves.

cards.headline: Jay Collins files lawsuit challenging James Fishback's eligibility for Florida governor's race
cards.teaser: The lawsuit argues Fishback does not meet Florida's constitutional requirement that a governor live in the state for at least seven years before being elected.
cards.body:
Lt. Gov. Jay Collins filed a lawsuit this week arguing that Republican gubernatorial candidate James Fishback does not meet Florida's constitutional requirement that a governor live in the state for at least seven years before being elected. Collins said he filed the challenge because election integrity matters. The legal complaint points to Fishback's ties to Washington, D.C., including allegations that he claimed a D.C. property as a primary residence and voted there in 2020.

Fishback denied that he is ineligible, arguing he was born and raised in Florida and accusing Collins of trying to damage his campaign. Without providing evidence, Fishback suggested that Collins is working in concert with Congressman Byron Donalds and said his campaign's first motion would call for Donalds and Collins to release all communications between their two campaigns. The court fight adds another layer of uncertainty to the GOP primary as mail ballots soon go out and the Aug. 18 primary approaches. Donalds has built significant momentum in the race, raising more than $90 million this cycle and securing endorsements from Attorney General James Uthmeier and Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia, both appointed by Gov. Ron DeSantis.

cards.headline: Woodson African American Museum of Florida to reopen with Smithsonian-linked exhibition as part of 20th anniversary
cards.teaser: The museum's newly renovated facility reopens July 11 with an America 250 exhibition. The Woodson was selected as one of only three Florida organizations to present the Many Voices One Nation exhibition.
cards.body:
The Woodson African American Museum of Florida's newly renovated museum is set to reopen July 11 as part of its 20th anniversary celebration, coinciding with the opening of a Smithsonian-linked America 250 exhibition. The Woodson was selected as one of only three Florida organizations to present the "Many Voices One Nation — Our Community" exhibition.

The museum's reopening marks a significant moment as the institution enters a new chapter with potential for a permanent home. Mayor Ken Welch selected The Burg Bid proposal as the city's preferred redevelopment plan for Tropicana Field and the surrounding Historic Gas Plant District. The $8.1 billion plan places The Woodson within Samuel Davis Park along a diagonal pedestrian corridor called the Legacy Link, where it would serve as "an anchor and a civic landmark for the Gas Plant District." The proposal emphasizes respect for the history of the former Gas Plant neighborhood, a predominantly Black community razed decades ago to make way for Tropicana Field. The team proposes preserving the original gas tank footprint within Samuel Davis Park and weaving historic references throughout the Legacy Link and other cultural amenities to tell the story of the community that once stood there.

hero.headline: Hobe Sound woman dies in Monday house fire ahead of her 47th birthday
hero.teaser: Misty Dawn White, 46, was found dead Monday after a fire broke out in her Hobe Sound home. Preliminary findings from the sheriff's office point to an electrical issue as a possible cause.
hero.body:
Misty Dawn White, 46, died in a house fire Monday at the home she shared with her fiancé in Hobe Sound. Authorities responded to the blaze and found White inside. Preliminary investigations by the sheriff's office suggest an electrical problem may have caused the fire, though the incident remains under active investigation. The flames destroyed numerous belongings owned by both White and her fiancé.

Nina Fenn, who had been friends with White for eight years, received the devastating news through a phone call from White's fiancé, Mark. "We received a call from Mark stating that Misty had passed away in a fire," Fenn said. In the days following the tragedy, Fenn returned to the scene to grieve and process the loss. "It's just a terrible shame and awful loss of life," she said. The community has responded by launching a fundraiser to help Mark rebuild after losing so many personal items in the fire. "It's completely a state of devastation," Fenn said.

Fenn remembered White as someone who made a lasting impact on those around her. "Misty was a Christian woman. She loved gardening and plants. She plays the piano," Fenn said. "She was always the first to lend a hand. She loves kids; she loves her kids. She loves people." White's compassion and generosity extended to everyone in her circle, and Fenn emphasized that these qualities defined who she was. "She's always been a good soul to me. She'll always be in our hearts," Fenn said.

The timing of White's death carries additional heartbreak for those who knew her. "Misty's birthday is the Fourth of July. So, she passed just a few days before her birthday," Fenn said. The loss is further complicated by the grief her fiancé is already carrying from a previous tragedy. "Mark lost his one and only child, Jacob, and lost him tragically. So, I just am trying whatever I can to support him," Fenn said. For Mark and White's loved ones, the coming weeks will require rebuilding both their home and their lives after this unexpected loss. Those who knew White say her memory will endure in the hearts of everyone she touched.

cards.headline: Martin County maritime teams deploy medics on two boats for Fourth of July weekend boating surge
cards.teaser: Martin County Maritime Response Unit is deploying two boats with medics on standby in the northern and southern parts of the county as hundreds of boaters celeb.
cards.body:
Martin County Maritime Response Unit is deploying two boats with medics on standby across the northern and southern parts of the county as hundreds of boaters take to local waterways to celebrate the Fourth of July weekend. Lt. Brett Harry with the Maritime Response Unit said the teams are prepared to respond to medical emergencies ranging from stubbed toes to cardiac events and potential spinal injuries.

Boaters launched from Sandsprit Park in Martin County on Friday, including Brendan and Ashley Shannon, who brought their young daughter and puppy onto the water. The Shannons said safety is their top priority when hitting the water. Lt. Harry urged boaters to keep their eyes on the water, designate a sober driver, and pack life vests, whistles and flotation devices before setting sail. "Just have fun and be safe," Harry said.

cards.headline: Martin County School Board fights judge's order to reinstate Spectrum Academy teacher Matt Theobald
cards.teaser: The Martin County School Board filed a court document Thursday challenging an administrative law judge's recommendation to reinstate Matt Theobald, a social studies teacher at Spectrum Academy suspended for Facebook comments about Charlie Kirk.
cards.body:
The Martin County School Board is pushing back against a judge's recommendation to reinstate Matt Theobald, a social studies teacher at Spectrum Academy since 2009 who was suspended last year following controversial social media comments about Charlie Kirk. In a Thursday court filing, the school board argued Administrative Law Judge Jodi-Ann Vanessa Livingstone erred in recommending Theobald get his job back, saying "numerous findings ... are not based upon competent substantial evidence." The board's attorney claims Theobald's Facebook post about Kirk was a "serious offense" and removing him was appropriate.

Theobald's comments labeled Kirk as racist, misogynistic and a neo-Nazi. According to an investigation report, Theobald admitted writing the comments about Kirk but said they were posted on his mother's private Facebook page "within a discussion among personal acquaintances" and were not intended for public view. In an order issued last month, Livingstone cited a recent Florida Fifth District Court of Appeal ruling that said disciplining a teacher for personal Facebook posts made off school grounds, on personal equipment, with no student involvement, violated the teacher's First Amendment rights. The judge also recommended Theobald be awarded back pay and benefits. The school board still has the final say on whether Theobald gets his job back.

hero.headline: Body of missing diver recovered near Fort Pierce Inlet
hero.teaser: Deputies found the body of a missing diver on the Florida coast near Fort Pierce Inlet.
hero.body:
The body of a missing diver was recovered on the Florida coast near Fort Pierce Inlet, according to a report from deputies. The recovery followed a search operation for the missing diver.

Deputies located the body in waters off the Fort Pierce Inlet area. The circumstances surrounding the diver's death remain under investigation by authorities.

cards.headline: Driver held teens at gunpoint after Orbeez pellet shooting in Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: A driver held teenagers at gunpoint after they shot Orbeez pellets at his car in Port St. Lucie, according to police.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police reported that a driver held teenagers at gunpoint following an incident where the teens shot Orbeez pellets at his vehicle. The confrontation occurred after the pellets struck the driver's car.

Police responded to the incident and are investigating the circumstances. The case involves both the pellet shooting and the armed response by the driver.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie approves land transfer for new Florida Turnpike interchange at Midway Road
cards.teaser: The Port St.
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of an ordinance last month to transfer 7 acres of land to the Florida Department of Transportation for a partial interchange on Florida's Turnpike in St. Lucie County. Scott Samples, strategic communications manager for Port St. Lucie, said there is a significant gap between current Turnpike entrances and exits in the city. He stated the interchange is designed to accommodate growth that has already occurred and growth expected over the next 20 to 50 years.

FDOT is constructing the $95 million Midway Road Widening Project to address congestion and safety. Crews are currently in the first phase, widening the road from two lanes to four lanes between Selvitz Road and Jenkins Road. The second widening phase from Jenkins Road to Glades Cut Off Road remains in the design phase, with construction anticipated to begin in Summer 2027. The partial Turnpike interchange is also still in the design phase. The project will add bike and pedestrian paths along with sidewalks. The city council will vote on final approval to transfer the land at an upcoming meeting.

cards.headline: Two rescued after boat sinks in St. Lucie County Intracoastal Waterway
cards.teaser: Two people were rescued after their boat sank in the Intracoastal Waterway in St. Lucie County.
cards.body:
Two individuals required rescue after their boat sank in the Intracoastal Waterway in St. Lucie County. Emergency responders successfully retrieved both people from the water.

Bodycam footage captured the rescue operation as crews responded to the sinking vessel. The two individuals were brought to safety following the boat's submersion in the waterway.

cards.teaser: Costco is planning its first Treasure Coast store in Port St. Lucie.
cards.body:
The retail warehouse chain Costco plans to open its first location on the Treasure Coast in Port St. Lucie. The store will be the first Costco presence in the tri-county area.

The Port St. Lucie location represents an expansion of the warehouse retailer into the regional market. Details about the store's timeline and specific location are part of the company's development plans for the area.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce woman recognized for supporting Little Free Libraries
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce woman received recognition for her support of Little Free Libraries in the community.
cards.body:
A Fort Pierce resident was honored for her contributions to supporting Little Free Libraries in the area. The recognition acknowledges her efforts to promote community access to books through the Little Free Library network.

The Little Free Library initiative provides neighborhood book exchanges where residents can take and share books. The Fort Pierce woman's work has helped sustain and expand these community resources in the local area.

cards.teaser: The Legacy Lions Football team in Port St. Lucie has updated standings for the current season.
cards.body:
Legacy Lions Football, representing Port St. Lucie, has current season standings available through Sports Illustrated. The team's performance metrics reflect their position in the competitive landscape.
