hero.headline: Insurance company denies breast cancer patient's reconstruction surgery hours before procedure
hero.body:
Beth Clark, 48, was denied coverage for breast reconstruction surgery less than 24 hours before her procedure was scheduled to begin. Three months earlier, Clark had been diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma, the most common type of breast cancer, and underwent a full double bilateral mastectomy. The denial from Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield rejected coverage for the reconstruction using GalaFlex surgical mesh, claiming the treatment is still considered investigational with insufficient evidence that it improves health outcomes.

The surgical mesh at the center of the dispute has become controversial in the medical community. While the FDA has approved GalaFlex for some uses throughout the body, it has not approved it specifically for breast reconstruction, making it an off-label treatment. In a 2023 letter to health care providers, the FDA stated that the efficacy and safety of GalaFlex for breast cancer patients have not been determined. Despite this regulatory status, Dr. Alicia Billington, Clark's plastic surgeon, uses GalaFlex mesh on most of her breast reconstruction patients and says it produces the least amount of complications compared to other options. Billington has joined other physicians in publicly criticizing insurers on social media, calling for them to review published literature demonstrating the treatment's success.

Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield responded by stating it regularly reviews medical coverage policies to ensure they align with medical evidence and current treatment standards. The company emphasized that without FDA approval for breast reconstruction, the mesh does not meet its coverage requirements, though it covers many other evidence-based alternatives. The insurer also noted that Clark retains the right to appeal the decision and confirmed ongoing communication with her physician. The company's position reflects broader industry standards around FDA approval and coverage decisions.

Despite the denial, Clark received her reconstruction surgery with GalaFlex mesh about a week later after her surgeon found a way to make the procedure happen. Clark and Billington continue fighting the insurance denial. Last year, Cigna became the first and only major insurer to begin approving GalaFlex for breast reconstruction after investigative reporting highlighted stories of patients being denied the procedure. A new bill has been introduced to modernize the Women's Health and Cancer Rights Act, a federal law designed to protect breast cancer patients from being denied treatments during their cancer treatment journeys.

cards.headline: Juno Beach residents push for fence replacement at JB-7 beach access after 2023 removal
cards.teaser: Colony Condos residents say beachgoers are cutting through their private property at the JB-7 public walkway since the town removed the old fence in 2023 for safety reasons. A fix could cost the town thousands of dollars.
cards.body:
Residents at the Colony Condos say people using the JB-7 public walkway are cutting through their private property since the town removed the old fence in 2023 for safety reasons. Without it, only bushes separate the public access path from private land. Lori Hill, a Colony resident, said the problem peaks in summer with cars parking in private spots and people cutting through bushes with coolers, fishing rods, and lawn chairs. Hill said residents used to confront trespassers but now call police after getting rude responses.

The dispute came before the Juno Beach Town Council at a recent meeting, where a town official noted the town is not obligated to install a fence. Vice Mayor Pro Tem DD Halpern suggested a lower-cost solution, proposing a combination of split rail and shrubs. Hill said residents are hopeful the town will reinstall the fence so they can have their landscaping and private parking back. The council agreed to take up the fence question as part of its upcoming budget discussions on July 15. Not everyone sees a major issue, with beachgoer Michael House saying he walks to JB-7 from a public lot a couple of blocks away and has never witnessed the problems residents describe.

cards.headline: Riviera Beach named only Florida city to receive 2026 All-America City Award
cards.teaser: Riviera Beach was selected as one of just 10 communities in the United States to receive the 2026 All-America City Award from the National Civic League. The city was the only Florida community honored this year.
cards.body:
The City of Riviera Beach received the 2026 All-America City Award from the National Civic League, becoming one of just 10 U.S. communities selected for the honor and the only Florida city chosen this year. The award recognizes communities that bring residents, local government, businesses and organizations together to solve local challenges and create lasting change. The award was announced during the National Civic League conference in Denver, where Riviera Beach leaders presented the city's efforts to strengthen community engagement. Mayor Douglas Lawson called the recognition a proud moment, saying "Little old Riviera Beach is one of the biggest, brightest, shining stars." Lawson said the city earned the award through a long-term effort to revitalize Riviera Beach and improve quality of life for residents.

Riviera Beach's application highlighted three programs designed to increase civic participation: the Riviera Beach Youth Council, which helps high school students become involved in civic leadership and advocacy; the Citizens Leadership Academy, a civic education initiative with a 98% completion rate; and the Neighborhood Reclaim Home Rehabilitation Program, which provides mini-grants to longtime homeowners. Councilwoman KaShamba Miller-Anderson credited residents for the honor, saying every event, project and challenge overcome happens because the community shows up for one another. The All-America City Award has been presented annually since 1949 and is considered one of the nation's most respected civic honors.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County schools earn third consecutive A rating from state with record 93.5% graduation rate
cards.teaser: The School District of Palm Beach County received an A rating from the Florida Department of Education for the third year in a row. The district achieved a record-setting 93.5% graduation rate.
cards.body:
The School District of Palm Beach County received an "A" rating from the Florida Department of Education for the third consecutive year, with 143 district-operated schools, or 84%, rated "A" or "B," up from 120 schools the previous year. The district achieved a record-setting 93.5% graduation rate. School districts and schools receive letter grades from the Florida Department of Education based on several factors, including student performance on state tests, graduation rates and student performance on advanced coursework. District leaders said 86% of seniors participated in college-level coursework, taking at least one Advanced Placement, International Baccalaureate, Cambridge Advanced International Certificate of Education, or Dual Enrollment course. In addition, 144 recent graduates earned an associate degree alongside their high school diploma.

S.D. Spady Elementary School in Delray Beach made a dramatic leap from a "C" rating last year to an "A" this year. Principal Rona Tata, who has spent the last 15 years as principal after serving five years as assistant principal, said staff began taking a closer look at the foundation of student learning three years ago by modifying the school's early childhood curriculum program. Many of those students are now in third grade and performing at higher levels. Spady Elementary was one of four district schools to improve from a "C" rating to an "A" this year, along with Dwight D. Eisenhower K-8, Glade View Elementary and West Gate Elementary.

cards.headline: Saint Andrew's Scots football targets state title after 10-2 season and district championship
cards.teaser: The Saint Andrew's Scots finished last season with a 10-2 record and a district title but lost in the second round of playoffs. The team is preparing for a more demanding schedule this fall.
cards.body:
The Saint Andrew's Scots finished last season with a 10-2 record and a district title, but a second-round playoff exit left the team feeling like more was within reach. Head football coach Jimmy Robertson noted that most of the seniors are four-year seniors who came from the middle school and have had a lot of success in their careers. With this veteran senior class leading the way, the program is leaning into a more demanding schedule this fall to compete at the next level.

Senior Jack Williams said the team wanted to take the program to the next level with a challenging schedule by playing against really good teams. Senior Jack Whelche said a better year means going farther in the playoffs, adding that going undefeated in the season does not matter if the team keeps losing in the second round of the playoffs. Senior Edmyer St. Jean said the daily grind of summer workouts adds up as something to look forward to, providing motivation to work harder so the team can see positive results and break their record when the season comes.

cards.headline: Boca Raton High School band to represent Florida at National Independence Day Parade in Washington
cards.teaser: The Boca Raton Community High School band will march down the National Mall on July 4 at 10:30 a.m. as Florida's representative at the National Independence Day Parade. Only bands nominated by state officials are invited to the event.
cards.body:
The Boca Raton Community High School band has earned a coveted spot in Washington, D.C.'s National Independence Day Parade, representing the entire state of Florida. On July 4 at 10:30 a.m., the students will march a full mile along the National Mall, from Constitution Avenue to Independence Avenue. Only bands nominated by state officials receive invitations to this prestigious event.

Junior Lola Cabezas acknowledged the pressure of performing before millions of viewers but expressed confidence the band will rise to the occasion. Senior Stephin Restivo said the team is laser-focused on nailing every detail, emphasizing that marching, timing, and consistent sound execution are critical since everyone will be watching. Band Director Jenn Girdlestone said she has full confidence in her students to put their best foot forward and represent the country well. Senior Lily Schaffer called the opportunity amazing, saying it showcases how much the program has grown. The parade will be streamed live on YouTube for those watching from home.

cards.headline: Fourth of July cookout costs up 4% this year with ground beef and buns seeing biggest increases
cards.teaser: A holiday meal for 10 now costs $73.82, up 4% from a year ago, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation's Summer Cookout Cost Survey. Ground beef is up 5.5% and buns are up 7.7%.
cards.body:
A Fourth of July cookout for 10 people now costs $73.82, up 4% from a year ago, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation's Summer Cookout Cost Survey. The survey points to inflation as the driving force behind the increases. Ground beef prices have risen 5.5%, while buns are up 7.7%. Strawberries, hit hard by a Florida frost, have seen the steepest increase at 12.4%, and ice cream prices are up 5.3%.

Not all cookout staples have become more expensive. Potato prices are down this year, benefiting those planning to serve potato chips and salads. Corn prices have fluctuated, though locally grown corn from the Glades can offer better deals. Budgeting expert Andrea Woroch recommends shopping strategically by comparing prices across stores to find the best deals for your grocery list. She emphasizes that reducing food waste through meal planning is the most important step families can take to manage costs.
